paras: The police beating of George Bailey was an alleged assault in Washington, D.C., in late July or early August 1890, in which Officer John H. Trammell of the Second Precinct was charged with clubbing Bailey, a Black man, while arresting him. District Attorney Armes dropped the assault charge against the officer, and Black residents took up the case at protest meetings against police violence that August.

That summer Black Washingtonians met at the Second Baptist Church to discuss what the Daily Critic called "recent outrages alleged to have been committed by the police upon the negroes." Alongside Bailey's case, they took up Officer Dyer's shooting of Charles Gray, alias Spotts, an alleged burglar, and Dr. Coughlin's shooting of three Black boys found taking pears.

According to the Evening Star, Trammell arrested Bailey on O Street and, it was charged, struck him on the head with his club so hard that a physician had to stitch his scalp. Bailey himself was brought before the Police Court, where, by the Star's garbled account, he was fined $5; the same passage mentions a charge against him of assaulting the officer.

Bailey swore out a warrant charging Trammell with assault, and about a dozen witnesses were summoned. On August 2, however, Armes entered a nolle prosequi, reasoning that Judge Miller had "virtually tried the case" when Bailey appeared in court the day before.

The Critic reported that the city's Black residents were "again very much disgusted" with Armes. On the evening of August 5 the executive committee of the Citizens' Protective Association named R. D. Rufflin, E. M. Hewlett and W. C. Martin to a committee on grievances, complained of Armes's action and referred the case to a mass meeting set for the following Monday. Organizers planned resolutions demanding that the charge against Trammell be called up again and tried, but no report of the Monday meeting or a retrial was found.
In September the Critic wrote that Trammell had "earned a reputation within the past year or so, for his extra officiousness," citing other arrests but not Bailey's.

The case appeared only in two Washington dailies, and no Black-press report of it was found. The Daily Critic first ran the news under the headline "Protecting the Officer," treating the nolle as a shield for Trammell. Three days later the same paper headed its notice of the protest "It's Too Bad. The Police Wont Let the Negroes Do as They Please," while repeating the claim that Trammell "brutally beat a colored gentleman named Bailey" and passing on a rumor of arrests for "incendiary or anarchistic expressions." The Evening Star, under "Assaults on Colored People," gave the fullest account of the injury but attributed it throughout with "it is charged" and "alleged."

reader.title: Police beating of George Bailey
bases: A police officer, Trammell, was charged with clubbing Bailey on the head during an arrest (A1, A3); no crowd or mob was involved.

Two separate Washington dailies report Bailey's assault charge against Trammell and its nolle pros (A1, A2, A3); the beating itself is reported as a claim ('it is claimed', 'it is charged') but no report denies it.

accounts.gist: The Citizens' Protective Association and an indignation meeting treated the case as one of several police and civilian assaults on Black residents and demanded it be retried.

framing.detail: The Daily Critic first ran the nolle under 'Protecting the Officer' and noted Black disgust with Armes (A1), then mocked the protest as 'The Police Wont Let the Negroes Do as They Please' while repeating that Trammell 'brutally beat' Bailey (A2).
The Evening Star headed its report 'Assaults on Colored People' and attributed the injury to the complaint ('it is charged', 'alleged').
In September the Critic attacked Trammell's 'extra officiousness' in a column on police abuses, without mentioning Bailey.
